cards.title: Test TikTok creative organically before spending ad budget
cards.summary: Run a six-step Spark Ads loop that posts videos organically first, waits 5-7 days for full organic reach, then amplifies only the proven winners with paid budget.
cards.use_when: You are planning TikTok acquisition creative for a store and deciding which videos deserve paid spend versus which should be left to run free.
steps: Produce three or more videos at a time, either in-house or by briefing influencers, so you always have a batch to compare rather than judging a single creative.
Post them to your own TikTok account, or have the influencers post to theirs, so organic performance data accumulates.

Wait five to seven days before deciding. The presenter's reasoning is that new TikTok posts typically see organic traffic concentrated in the first couple of days and roughly a week-long life cycle — you don't want to pay to reach people who would have seen it free.

After the wait, judge each video on the results it produced: sales attributed to that post, follows, and engagement. The presenter's own example shows three influencer videos at 2.3M, 15K and 8M organic views — pick the clear performer to amplify. In a second example the differentiator was engagement, not raw views.
Run the one or two winners as Spark Ads, then repeat the cycle with a new batch. The loop scales: post 20 videos and take the top 10-30% as ads instead of three.
Expect the creative selection to be the main lever — in the presenter's account, 400+ SKUs and multiple videos existed, but only the organic winners were worth paying to distribute.
caveats: The 5-7 day wait and the 'first two days' signal are the presenter's observations about typical TikTok behavior, not guaranteed benchmarks; verify against your own account's data.
View counts and engagement are proxies — the presenter also references sales and follows as selection criteria, so prefer whichever metric maps to your objective.

cards.title: Set up a Spark Ad from your own organic post
cards.summary: Inside Ads Manager's ad creative step, select TikTok post to run an existing organic video as a Spark Ad from your own account.
cards.use_when: You have an organic TikTok post from your own profile that performed well and you want to put paid amplification behind it.
steps: Build the campaign as normal through objective and targeting; Spark Ads can be run against essentially any objective, including the sales objective.
At the ad creative step, navigate to the video/creative selection and choose the TikTok post source.
Use the account dropdown to pick the TikTok account you want to pull posts from.
Select the specific organic post from the list. If your posts don't appear, your TikTok ad account is not linked to your TikTok account — fix the linkage before continuing.
Confirm to attach the post as your Spark Ad creative, then finish the remaining campaign setup.
Note the destination URL is editable, so you control where the ad traffic lands even though the ad displays from your own profile.
caveats: The exact interface labels shift over time — verify the current TikTok Ads Manager layout before following these clicks.
The source demonstrates this flow in a specific ad account; account-linking requirements may differ by region.

cards.title: Run an influencer's video as a Spark Ad using an ad authorization code
cards.summary: Request a TikTok post code from the creator, then add it via 'add post' in the ad creative step to run their video as a paid ad from their profile.
cards.use_when: An influencer posted a video with your product and you want to amplify it with paid spend as a Spark Ad from their handle.
steps: In the ad creative step, open the TikTok post source and use the 'add post' option, which prompts for a TikTok post code.
Instruct the creator: open the video they posted for you, tap the three dots, choose ad settings, and turn on ad authorization.
Tell them to set the authorization duration to 365 days (the presenter's recommendation) so you can run the ad as long as possible.
Once authorized and saved, they generate an ad authorization code, tap manage code and copy it, then send you the code.
Paste the code into the post code field in Ads Manager and continue — the video appears and can be added to your ad library and confirmed as creative.
Set the destination URL so traffic goes to the page you want, even though the ad runs from the influencer's profile.
caveats: Authorization is creator-controlled; the creator can adjust or decline, so agree terms before relying on the footage.
The exact menu names inside the TikTok app change — verify current steps with the creator when you send instructions.
A long authorization period does not guarantee continued performance; the ad still competes on creative merit.

cards.title: Why Spark Ads engagement accrues to the organic post
cards.summary: Likes, comments and engagement on a Spark Ad also appear on the original organic post, creating one amplified asset rather than a separate ad unit.
cards.use_when: You are deciding whether to run creator content as a Spark Ad versus a standalone ad creative, and want to understand the compounding effect on the original post.
steps: Recognize that engagement generated by the paid ad — likes and comments — also shows on the organic post, so the ad and the organic asset reinforce each other.
Plan creative selection around posts that already show strong engagement, since paid amplification adds to rather than replaces that interaction profile.
Because the ad runs from the creator's handle, evaluate whether their profile credibility and audience fit the product before committing budget.
Use the editable destination URL to route paid traffic to the page you control, separating 'who it appears from' (creator) from 'where it lands' (your store).
Budget the creator relationship around long authorization windows (the presenter suggests 365 days) so the compounding engagement keeps benefiting a single asset.
Treat Spark Ads as one asset with two distribution layers — organic reach first, paid amplification second — rather than two separate creative lines to manage.
caveats: The presenter's example mixes co-marketing with a partner profile, so results depend on the creator's existing audience and posting cadence. None of the view or engagement figures in the source are benchmarks.

cards.title: Stand up the TikTok Shop accounts needed before running Shop ads
cards.summary: Running TikTok Shop / GMV Max ads requires a Seller Center, a linked Business Center and Ads Manager, plus GMV Max authorization and admin access to the shop.
cards.use_when: You are preparing an ecommerce store to sell directly inside TikTok and need to know which accounts and permissions must exist before launch.
steps: Create a TikTok Seller Center account (separate from Business Center and Ads Manager) — this is what manages listings, orders, logistics, the storefront, seller-side promotions, affiliate recruitment and shop analytics.
Confirm you have a Business Center account and an Ads Manager account; the Seller Center is the piece specifically for running the shop.
Link the TikTok Shop to the Business Center, and make sure the ad account you'll use has GMV Max authorization for that shop.
Ensure you hold admin access to the shop account, since critical settings live behind it.
Use one consistent email or phone number across your Shopify/WooCommerce account and the Seller Center — the presenter notes this makes account connection smoother.
Check current regional availability before planning GMV Max, since it was limited to specific locations at the time of recording — verify the current list.
caveats: GMV Max availability was region-restricted at the time of the source; the location list may change.
The presenter mentions a signup link with advertised rewards — that is promotional and not required for setup.

cards.title: Sync your Shopify catalog into TikTok Shop
cards.summary: Install the official TikTok app for Shopify to sync products, stock and pricing into your Seller Center instead of creating listings by hand.
cards.use_when: You are launching a TikTok Shop and want product listings, pricing and stock to flow from your existing ecommerce catalog rather than manual entry.
steps: In Seller Center, open the product listing methods (list a URL, bulk upload, or sync with other platforms such as Amazon, Shopify, eBay).
Choose the sync path, which sends you to an app store; search for the official provider app (in this case 'TikTok for Shopify') and install it, not a third-party clone.
Inside Shopify, click set up on the 'start selling on TikTok' option, then connect to your Seller Center shop account.
Beware the account-connection step asks for verification — email or phone — so use the same contact as your Seller Center signup.
Set shipping: the presenter recommends 'seller shipping' (use your Shopify settings) for most merchants, since fulfilling by TikTok is the alternative.
Map carriers and define warehouse pickup and return addresses in Seller Center; those must exist before you can sell.
After shipping is updated the products sync automatically, but some fail. Open the error view: examples include missing region of origin or other required fields, so complete every red-starred field.
Watch for restricted categories — the demo hits a cookware/dishes restriction that prevents approval on a demo account.
Check listing quality and drive each listing from 'fair' to the highest status, using TikTok's improve-listing-quality checklist for anything below 'good'.
Verify the product is live by searching your store name in TikTok and switching to the Shop tab.
caveats: Restricted product categories can block listing regardless of how complete the data is.
Synced stock and price flow from Shopify, so source-of-truth errors propagate to TikTok.
Interface steps in both Shopify and Seller Center change; verify current flows.

cards.title: Read the Seller Center dashboard and fix listings below good quality
cards.summary: The Seller Center home, products and marketing tabs surface orders, violations, low stock and listing quality issues you must resolve to sell effectively.
cards.use_when: You are operating a live TikTok Shop and need a routine for catching operational and listing problems before they cost sales.
steps: Check the home tab for recent performance and the to-do list: orders ready to ship, pending returns, violations, low stock, and negative reviews. Treat reviews as a marketplace signal to respond to.
Open the orders view to see current orders, shipped, completed, pending, returns and free shipping obligations.
In products, review active, under review, needs-attention and deactivated listings alongside stock, price and listing quality.
Click into any listing rated below good (e.g. 'fair') and follow the issue list to improve it; use the improve-listing-quality to-do to batch-fix everything below that threshold.
In the marketing tab, open shop design to see how the storefront renders and the current store conversion rate.
Test alternative shop templates if available, then return to the same conversion-rate view to see whether the change actually moved the rate.
Set up the affiliate side (open and target collaborations) so creators can begin producing tagged videos for the catalog.
caveats: The presenter's instruction to optimize every listing to the highest quality score is a recommendation, not a measured guarantee of sales lift.
Conversion rate in this view reflects the store overall, so a design change's effect must be read over time, not from one snapshot.

cards.title: Structure open and target affiliate collaborations with commission tiers
cards.summary: Offer open collaborations at a fixed commission to anyone who drives a sale, and send target collaborations with custom rates to handpicked creators.
cards.use_when: You want to recruit TikTok creators to post tagged videos for your products without paying upfront for content that doesn't sell.
steps: Set up an open collaboration where the creator earns a commission (the presenter uses 20% as an example) only when they actually drive a sale — you pay nothing extra otherwise.
Decide whether the offer includes free products or a request flow, and whether samples are free or refundable.
Control sample requests: they arrive as requests you approve or reject, so a creator can't simply pull samples.
Set thresholds so only qualified creators can request samples — for example a minimum follower count (the presenter cites 10,000) or a minimum revenue driven (e.g. $100, $1,000, $10,000).
For target collaborations, send a batch invitation with a name, validity dates, contact details, a message, and the specific products.
Assign each handpicked creator a custom commission rate and optionally a flat fee; you can vary rates per creator (e.g. 24% vs 25%).

Add a separate shop ads commission rate that pays the creator when their content is amplified as a paid ad. The presenter recommends setting it lower than the standard rate (he cites around 5%) because you're adding ad spend on top.
caveats: Commission percentages and thresholds in the source are illustrative, not universal rules — set them from your own margin.
When reviewing sample requests, the source shows creators with attributes like post rate and 30-day GMV; those are creator-specific data points, not proof of future performance.

cards.title: Set up a GMV Max campaign that sells inside TikTok
cards.summary: GMV Max runs a single campaign that tests all tagged product videos, optimizes against a target product ROI, and checks buyers out inside TikTok.
cards.use_when: You have a TikTok Shop with tagged creator videos and want paid distribution that drives direct in-app purchases.
steps: Enter via the campaigns flow: sales objective → TikTok Shop destination → continue to GMV Max, or use the GMV Max tab directly.
Select the shop from the dropdown when creating a campaign. If it doesn't appear, link the Shop to your Business Center first.
Choose promote products or promote live. For a new account, the presenter recommends not promoting all products — start with your top sellers.

Note the constraint: you can only run one GMV Max campaign per product, so a single campaign covering many products limits future flexibility. The presenter's default is to take the top 20% of products (using historical order data to rank) into one campaign. If you have no sales history, you must estimate the top products yourself.

Set product ROI. TikTok suggests a target (the source shows 1.2, which the presenter notes is often below break-even for ecommerce). The presenter takes TikTok's recommendation and adds 1.0 to it (1.2 → 2.2), then watches impressions over the next few days and lowers it if nothing is delivering. Setting ROI too high can stop ads from showing at all.
Set the daily budget at roughly double your target cost per acquisition (the example: $30 target CPA → $60/day). TikTok will always push for more spend than you set.

Adjust special promotion days: left at defaults, TikTok can raise budget by 50% and multiply it up to 10x, which turned a $60 budget into a $360 maximum in the example. The presenter narrows it to 50% with a 1x limit, keeping the setting on for genuine holiday demand.

For ad creative, the presenter recommends leaving auto-select on so TikTok rapidly tests incoming tagged videos, pauses underperformers and amplifies better-ROI ones. You can instead manage specific authorized posts, affiliate posts, custom posts or uploaded videos.
caveats: The 'add 1.0 to TikTok's recommended ROI' and 'double target CPA' rules are the presenter's heuristics, not verified benchmarks.
The one-campaign-per-product limit is a structural constraint that shapes how you group products.
Auto-select means TikTok chooses creative; you trade control for automated testing.

cards.title: Monitor GMV Max creative performance and boost winning ads
cards.summary: Use GMV Max analytics and the creatives view to see which videos are delivering, and apply a creative boost to push extra daily budget behind winners.
cards.use_when: Your GMV Max campaign is live and you need to see which tagged videos are actually running and where to add incremental spend.
steps: Open the campaign analytics and find the product list with availability, then use view creative to see the videos attached to each product and their statuses.

Interpret statuses: in queue (ready to be tested for conversion potential), learning phase, delivering, and not delivering (tested and no longer producing results, so TikTok pauses it automatically). All of this happens without manual intervention.
When a video is delivering strong return, apply a creative boost by clicking that ad and requesting a daily boost of at least $10/day, with an optional end date.
Account for the boost stacking on top of campaign spend — a $60/day campaign plus a $10 boost becomes a $70/day maximum.

Use the creatives view to see how many creators are producing videos and each creator's gross revenue contribution, so you can identify which creators and individual ads deserve their own dedicated campaign.
Take repeatedly winning videos and run them in their own GMV Max campaign where the one-campaign-per-product rule permits.
caveats: Creative boost minimum is $10/day and is additional to campaign budget — do not treat it as a reallocation.
Statuses and analytics views are interface-dependent; verify current labels in Ads Manager.
The source's $4,000 spend / $12,000 revenue example (~3 ROAS, described by the presenter as 'not awesome') is an individual case, not a performance standard.

cards.title: Build retargeting audiences from website, engagement and shop activity
cards.summary: Use TikTok's audience manager to build custom audiences from pixel events, video engagement and TikTok Shop activity, then exclude purchasers to avoid wasted spend.
cards.use_when: You want to run TikTok remarketing to store visitors, content engagers or shop visitors and need to define the right audience rules.
steps: Make sure your TikTok pixel is installed and linked to the ad account before building audiences.
In Ads Manager, go to tools → audience manager → create audiences, and choose custom audience.

For website traffic audiences, define the action (page view, add to cart, initiate checkout, purchase) and select the pixel source. You can add a URL-contains rule so only a specific page type qualifies — for example the presenter references targeting pages containing 'product' to reach product-page visitors.
Add an exclusion for purchasers: exclude users who completed a purchase in the last 30 days from a site-visitor audience, so you don't pay to re-reach customers you already converted.
Keep auto-refresh on so the audience is refreshed periodically (the presenter references a 30-day refresh).

Leave off the option to expand the audience with machine-learning-identified users — the presenter prefers knowing he is actually remarketing, arguing that adding lookalike-style expansion defeats the purpose and is no different from broad targeting.
Expect a delay before the audience is usable — initially it shows as unavailable and typically takes around 24 hours to match.

Build lookalike audiences from a strong source, ideally a purchasers-based custom audience, choosing a narrow/balanced/broad option (the presenter usually picks balanced) and setting the target location.
caveats: Auto-refresh interval and the 24-hour match time are the source's observations; platform behavior may vary.
The choice to leave off audience expansion is the presenter's opinion and a trade-off, not a universal best practice — expanding may increase reach.

cards.title: Run TikTok retargeting campaigns with budget-tiered audience structure
cards.summary: Apply the retargeting audiences in a sales campaign via manual targeting, and scale the number of retargeting and re-engagement campaigns as budget grows.
cards.use_when: You have built TikTok retargeting audiences and want a campaign structure that matches your monthly ad budget.
steps: Create a campaign with the sales objective and website traffic destination continuation, then at the audience step switch to manual targeting.

Under custom audiences, use the include dropdown to add the audiences you built (e.g. website visitors last 30 days, or a lookalike once populated), then continue through the rest of the campaign build as normal.
At budgets around $3,000 or less, the presenter recommends one prospecting campaign testing two audiences and one retargeting campaign for website visitors in the last 30 days.

As budget grows, add narrower retargeting tiers such as website visitors (last 7 days) who did not purchase, and add-to-cart in the last 30 days, potentially with different offers or promotions to bring people back.

At larger budgets (the presenter cites ~$10K+), add a dedicated re-engagement campaign targeting people who engage with your content, and run the GMV Max campaign alongside retargeting so the campaign types work together to scale.
Consider adding a lookalike built from your purchasers audience once the source custom audience has populated.
caveats: The $3,000 and $10K figures are the presenter's budget-tier heuristics for structuring campaigns, not derived benchmarks.
Lookalikes require a populated source audience before they can be created.
The presenter's view that expansion/expansion-based targeting is essentially broad targeting is an opinion; test in your account.
